subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA U.S. FREE TRADERESCINDING OF EXISTING COUNTERVAILING DUTIES
speechtext:
1 am worried as well because the Government has not clearly stated the objective it seeks to achieve from a free trade arrangement. It has not clearly stated the details of such an agreement, or the sectors which it would favour or disfavour. I heard the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) speak on Cross Country Check-up on Sunday last. He referred to Auto Pact as free trade. It is not free trade. I agree with the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) that the Minister, his Party and his colleagues are misleading the public about what this crucial question is all about.
I am concerned as well because-

-in Quebec we have a saying that one should not be more Catholic than the Pope. And in this debate on free trade, I often get the impression we are doing just that.
I wish the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) would stay for a few minutes, because I have a few comments I would like him to hear, especially on the need for a good post-secondary education system in this country so that we can compete with the United States and other countries on world markets. I will get to that in a few seconds, if he could wait. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker-

I think there is a tendency in this country for us to be holier than the Pope, as we say, in our approach to trade issues. We continually focus on what we might have to give up in a trade arrangement with the Americans, on what constitutes a subsidy or on what is unfair competition in our practices in Canada. Every single item is mentioned in the media. We refer to the Unemployment Insurance Program as possibly being a subsidy in certain regions of the country. We refer to our regional development policies. These questions are on the front pages of our newspapers on a daily basis. We have a masochistic attitude about it.
I remember about two years ago when Bombardier was trying to negotiate a sale of subway cars to New York City, which it ultimately successfully negotiated. A question arose as to whether or not financing furnished by the Export Development Corporation might constitute an unfair subsidy. Canadian reporters went down to the United States. They talked to local Congressmen and said to them: "Here is the Export Development Corporation in Canada giving Bombardier a subsidy. Do you think it is fair?" What answer do you think the Congressmen in the United States gave, Mr. Speaker? Contrast that situation with what happens in the United States. Do we see articles in U.S. papers stating that this or that measure is protectionist, or that the U.S. defence industry favours American companies? Not at all. The approval of the U.S, Senate Finance Committee, which made headlines and which was the first item on the news here in Canada, attracted little attention in the United States. For the Americans we are but small potatoes. It is this imbalance between our two countries which gives me great cause for concern. I feel that
Supply
the deck is stacked against us at the very outset because of the different sides of our two countries.
As I said earlier, the Government has failed to state its objectives in any more than a general way. I ask myself why. Is this part of its negotiating strategy? Or is it because the Government does not have any objectives? Personally, I think it is the latter. There is an absence of objectives. I listened to the last two speakers, members of the Conservative Party, who spoke in the House. In listening to them one would understand that free trade is seen by the Conservative Government as a substitute for a broad range of policies which are required to make Canada prosper. To them it is seen as the answer to all our problems, a panacea. Free trade is used by the Government as a mask to hide a series of incoherent policy decisions.
Several minutes ago my colleague from Windsor mentioned Hyundai, a Korean manufacturer setting up business in Canada. The Government gave Hyundai millions of dollars. Yet the representatives of that company said that they did not even want it. They did not even ask for a subsidy, but we were falling over ourselves trying to show that we created jobs in this particular industry. We did so regardless of the problems of over-capacity already in the industry and regardless of the fact that they were not asked to comply with the provisions of the Auto Pact. Millions of dollars were poured into an industry without any thought or concern for an over-all policy or for the over-all benefit which would accrue to Canadians.
The capital gains exemption of $500,000 in a taxpayer's lifetime is a boon for the rich. Every stockbroker, investment dealer and financial adviser in the country tells us that this measure will not achieve any substantial investment in the risky areas of our economy. The Government is willing to put money into the area but, as I said earlier, we are neglecting our human resources.
A Bill which is before Parliament today, Bill C-96, deals with post-secondary education and health, the established programs financing. In this Bill the Government is washing its hands of post-secondary education. We are cutting some $8 billion out of transfer payments which would otherwise have gone to the provinces for health and post-secondary education.

I would have liked to put the question directly to the Secretary of State. How are we going to compete with the United States if we do not have a good post-secondary education system in this country? Can we compete with the United States without world-class universities? Can we compete with the United Stated and the Japanese and the Europeans without centres of excellence in this country? What is the federal Government's role, Mr. Speaker? Why has the federal Government completely abdicated its responsibilities in this area?

Several months ago I read about three super computers which were being furnished to three different universities in the United States. I believe one was in New York State,

May 13, 1986
Supply
another in Illinois and the third in California. The computers were being completely paid for by companies such as IBM, Kodak and Sperry. Why? The head offices of these companies are located in that country. They benefit from the research which is conducted at those universities. Their offices are located close to these universities. When do members of the Conservative Party think that companies such as IBM, Sperry and Kodak will finance research in Canadian industry or in Canadian universities in the same magnitude as they do in the United States? We have a tradition of Government involvement in building this country which is being totally ignored by the Conservative Party.
In the face of this absence of clarity, this absence of policy from Government, it was refreshing to see a statement last week put out by the Science Council of Canada in which it pointed out some of the things that Canadians should watch for as we undertake these bilateral trade negotiations. Earlier, I mentioned the absence of information regarding policies which the United States has which benefit and give an unfair advantage to its industries. The Science Council of Canada pointed out that, among other things, in the United States defence contracts make up a substantial component of regional development support, and much of the support for industry does not appear as direct budget outlay. Second, when dealing with non-tariff barriers, the U.S. market is far more protected than Canada. In 1982, the United States sectors protected overtly by non-tariff barriers covered 34 per cent of the market for American manufacturers. This shold be compared to the figure in Canada of just 10 per cent, the figure of 7 per cent in Japan and the figure of 20 per cent in West Germany. Canada is a most open economy when it comes to non-tariff barriers.
In a section of the study entitled "The U.S. Challenge", the Science Council pointed out that 55 per cent of all research and development in the United States is funded by the Government compared to 50 per cent in Canada. This is contrary to what we hear every day of the week. The bulk of this research and development is limited to defence, which of course will not be discussed during these negotiations. Defence was specifically excluded from the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Defence spending had grown to 65 per cent of federally funded research and development in the United States in 1984. In 1984, some $32 billion of federal research expenditures were employed for defence-related activities.
There are more interesting facts. Within the U.S. Department of Defense budget, less than 10 per cent of contracts are publicly advertised and 40 per cent are signed with companies that have a complete monopoly on the equipment. How does one expect Canadian companies to compete in that kind of a market? Foreign companies are not even allowed to bid on some of these prime contracts. Canadian advanced technology companies are denied access to SDI briefings. The Science Council study also points out that at the state level, there are so many initiatives to promote technological innovation that in
1984, the Office of Technology Assessment was unable to provide a comprehensive inventory of these programs.
In the military sector of the aerospace industry, American companies have a number of advantages. First, they have open access to bidding on defence contracts. Second, they have greater R and D support than Canadian companies. About 70 per cent of R and D costs are paid for by defence contracts in the United States versus only 30 per cent in Canada. Third, the cost of machinery is covered by Department of Defense contracts in the United States. Fourth, in terms of information access, several U.S. government-sponsored computer information systems are accessible only to U.S. users.
How are Canadian companies to get access to this information and these contracts? There is only one real way to get access, and that is, to join the United States, to become American. I am telling you today, Mr. Speaker, that under a free trade arrangement with the United States, we will not be given access to the bulk of U.S. defence contracts. We could have the best negotiators in the world on our side, and I give all due credit to the man heading the Canadian negotiating team, Mr. Reisman, but when it comes down to the crunch, Canadians will not be given total access.
The Science Council of Canada sets out four policy principles which it believes should guide bilateral negotiations, and I would just like to summarize them briefly in conclusion. First, the Science Council believes that a free trade agreement should permit measures which would protect and favour infant industries on a carefully defined, temporary basis. Second, and this is the point to which I referred just a moment ago, all United States and Canadian Governments should allow what is referred to as national treatment to both U.S. and Canadian firms when bidding on all Government contracts, research awards and development assistance. This will not happen. Third, both parties must develop a clear understanding of the range of science, technology and industrial policy measures that each Government may take without the risk of countervailing action.
Again, referring to the comments I made earlier, we have even taken up the American jargon during the course of this debate. We refer to a level or a fair playing field, but I think that Canadians must understand that each sovereign country develops its own way of dealing with problems and concerns. Canadians must demonstrate to Americans that just because an approach is a Canadian approach does not mean that it constitutes an unfair advantage, and that any deviation from American methods and approaches is not unfair just because it is not American. They have their particular distinctive ways of arriving at solutions as do we. We should be able to continue such an independent approach.
Fourth, and again I do not see this happening, both countries should provide equal access to briefings and Government-sponsored scientific and technical information systems to enable firms in both countries to respond promptly to government procurement opportunities. Again, I find it very difficult
May 13, 1986

to see this being totally opened up in the context of such negotiations.
1 understand that most of today's debate has dealt with the softwood lumber issue. I would hope that on another day in the near future, we would deal specifically with high technology and the future of high technology and its application to our traditional industries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA U.S. FREE TRADERESCINDING OF EXISTING COUNTERVAILING DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the Hon. Member who just spoke is aware of what precipitated today's debate. I would like to ask him a question regarding that. On May 8, the President of the United States sent a letter to Senator Pack-wood, the Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, a committee which tied in a 10-10 vote as to fast tracking free-trade negotiations with Canada which are to begin the middle of next week. In that letter, the President said that he will press for an expedited resolution to this problem independent of the comprehensive trade negotiations and moreover that the President promised to take unilateral trade action if the bilateral lumber talks fail. We have that ongoing process involving the President, the United States administration, and its Senate Finance Committee, and Canada's largest single industry, largest single source of balance of trade, and second or third largest industry in the Province of Quebec.
I should like to ask the Hon. Member what he thinks about what is happening now. Representatives of the industry lobby in the United States have suspended temporarily their filing of a petition for a countervailing duty against Canadian softwoods until next Monday, although they were told by the Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Baldridge, that the clock is already running, to which I made reference earlier today. Rather than having to wait the full 20 days for a ruling on whether or not a countervail process will go ahead, they will only have to wait 13 calendar days from next Monday.
My question concerns the point of today's debate-whether or not Canada is steaming in the right direction. I think some enormous errors have been made by the Conservative administration on this issue, but I should like to know from the Hon. Member what he and his Party think about the proposal which will be carried forward by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) to Washington tomorrow. I am referring to the appointment of a Canadian envoy with very specific terms of reference on which to negotiate at very high speed on behalf of a $26 billion Canadian industry. Does the Hon. Member and his Party think that that process is likely to succeed?
Do they think it appropriate that the volume and price of Canadian softwood products going to the United States should be negotiated by the Canadian and U.S. envoys?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA U.S. FREE TRADERESCINDING OF EXISTING COUNTERVAILING DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his questions. With regard to the specifics, I defer to members of my Party who have a more intimate knowledge of the questions than I do. However, in general terms it is difficult for me to say whether this approach will succeed.
Supply
In the letter to Mr. Packwood from the President, the President said that he planned to take action independent of the trade negotiations. That indicated to me that we do not have a clean launch and that the President is saying that they will look after American interests immediately and quickly. It is not the only area on which Americans want quick settlement. In fact there are a number of other areas.
I see our being in a position where the big guy is getting nasty and is shoving us around and we are giving in. There is a possibility that we will give in on a number of essential points even before the negotiations have begun.
I found it rather remarkable-and I did not see anything in the press today-that the news last night included an item indicating that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) would be tabling Canada's new policy in respect of generic drugs, whereas just two weeks ago he said that the legislation would not be introduced until the fall and that further negotiations were required with the provinces. How come the process has been speeded up all of a sudden? It seems to me that we are not seeing comprehensive negotiations. We are seeing a series of attempts to satisfy the Americans. They are pushing their weight and trying to settle items immediately in their favour. This prejudices the entire ensuing negotiations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA U.S. FREE TRADERESCINDING OF EXISTING COUNTERVAILING DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is speaking more anti-American rhetoric than I have heard for a long time. It really concerns me.
The Hon. Member said that we as a Government were putting forward all the things we were giving up. I have never heard the Government talk about giving up anything. It is the Opposition which raises all the so-called things we will be giving up in the negotiations. The Opposition's reaction has been nothing but a negative one to the whole issue. I think the Hon. Member was a little confused when he talked about what was being given up.
Also he said that we were small potatoes, yet the dissertations of Hon. Members opposite all day have indicated that the United States would countervail us to death because we were so important. As has been the case all day, we just keep hearing counter-arguments.
Also he talked about objectives. I have not heard any mention of objectives or policy from his Party. There certainly appears to be a great division in his Party on what should happen in the negotiations with the United States.
As well he talked about the absence of clarity in policy. Honest to Pete, he should look inward to the policies of his cohorts; it seems that they have policies on both sides of the line.
Also he referred to non-tariff barriers in the United States and 34 per cent of the market. However, he seemed to indicate that we should not be negotiating with the U.S. to remove those non-tariff barriers.

May 13, 1986

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA U.S. FREE TRADERESCINDING OF EXISTING COUNTERVAILING DUTIES
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I respectfully say to the Hon. Member that I do not think there is anything antiAmerican in my comments. I believe in taking a strong Canadian position. I believe in putting forward Canada's interest. I do not believe that our interests are always and inevitably totally associated with American interests, which Hon. Members of the Conservative Party seem to indicate.
Perhaps the Hon. Member should read what I said when I talked about what we have to give up. I was not saying that the Government was putting that forward. I was saying that there was an inevitable focus on that in our country and in our media because we are a much smaller country than the United States. The natural focus is on problems in Canada as opposed to those in the United States where Canadian trade with the U.S. is much less important than is our trade in our country, all proportions being respected.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 82-CANADA U.S. FREE TRADERESCINDING OF EXISTING COUNTERVAILING DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not a Canadian who does not realize that if Canada is to prosper, if people are to find work, and if our companies are to operate and make a profit, we require increasing trade between Canada and all other countries.
If we are to improve trade between Canada and other countries, we have to understand what are our needs, what are their needs, and particularly what are their policies to protect their people, just as we want to protect and improve the lot of Canadians.
We all know that grain farmers in western Canada are in a terrible situation. Many of them will be wiped out in the next few years, not because they cannot produce grain efficiently, but because of the actions of our traditional customers in western Europe who are members of the European Economic Community. They are subsidizing the production of grain in their countries so much that not only do they not purchase grain from us, but they compete in other markets with our farmers. Also we know that the new American policy of subsidizing export sales of grain for American farmers will destroy further markets for us.
The Government is urging us to sign quickly some kind of free trade deal with the United States. Just at the very time we are talking about that and we are lecturing Canadians that we should get on with the job and make concessions so that the Americans will agree to free trade between Canada and the U.S., the Americans are imposing countervailing duties on Canadians. They are proposing a 30 per cent countervail duty on softwood. That would affect British Columbia very quickly, but it is not just British Columbia that would be affected, the Atlantic provinces would also be affected. They have a forest
industry, as does my Province of Manitoba and the Province of Saskatchewan. We do not hear about the things that the Americans do to protect their forest industry.
A few weeks ago the Americans imposed a countervail duty of 5.8 per cent on East Coast fish. The U.S. Commerce Department supported that position. It listed 55 federal and provincial programs ranging from fisheries research grants to grants for shipbuilding as constituting countervail subsidies.
I have before me a document prepared by our External Affairs Department which lists a large number of programs which the U.S. Government has established to assist its fishing industry. Let me read from this document. It says under the heading Direct Subsidies, loan guarantees for construction, reconstruction or reconditioning of fishing vessels. Then we see under Federal Tax Deferrals the fishing vessel capital construction fund for vessel acquisition. This program effectively provides an interest-free loan from the U.S. Government equal to the federal income taxes which otherwise would have to be paid. Next is Operating Cost Assistance. The Fishermen's Protective Act provides funds for fishing vessel and gear damage. Then we find Additional Measures. The Nicholson Act forbids foreign vessels from landing directly in U.S. ports, thus forcing Canadian boats to land in Canada and ship overland by truck, thereby increasing Canadian costs and making the Canadian fish less "fresh" than the U.S. product.
That is what the Americans do, Mr. Speaker, but when the Americans put a countervailing duty on Canadian fish, I did not hear the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) saying to the Americans: "Hey, guys, you are doing the same thing as you are accusing us of doing." Not only did he not say it to the Americans, but he did not get up and tell Canadians how one-sided, how tunnel visioned, how unfair the Americans were during this so-called period of negotiations. He was silent. There was not a peep out of him. Why, Mr. Speaker? I believe he takes that attitude because he wants to sell this concept to the Canadian people and he knows that if they know the facts, they will not buy it.
The other day when my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), put some questions to the Government, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) answered by suggesting that my Leader and our Party were taking orders from the President of the Canadian Labour Congress, as if only labour is opposed to the free trade negotiations, as if only labour is worried that somehow in these negotiations Canadians would be hurt. Let me quote from a recent issue of the Winnipeg Free Press. I hope the Minister for International Trade will listen.
I want to put on the record the views, not of labour leaders in Manitoba, but of three farm leaders in Manitoba. These are not my concerns but their concerns. On April 24, 1986, in part the article quotes John Kuhl, Chairman of the Manitoba Vegetable Producers Marketing Board, as follows:
May 13, 1986

Manitoba vegetable growers cannot compete on equal terms with their American counterparts because of higher taxes, higher fuel prices and shorter growing seasons-
Next is Waldie Klassen, Chairman of the Manitoba Chicken Broiler Producers Marketing Board, who said:
As far as our industry is concerned it would have some far-reaching and devastating effects.
Most of our industry could disappear.
He was talking about free trade in agriculture. Then we have Jack Penner, President of the Keystone Agricultural Producers, an organization which represents all the producing groups of agriculture in Manitoba, who said he is worried:
-that agriculture has been combined with the food and beverage sector for negotiating purposes, which will make it harder to protect agricultural interests.
Our concern is that agriculture not be used to gain other advantages.
Who is he complaining about, Mr. Speaker? Who ignored agriculture? Who put somebody from the food industry as chairman of the advisory committee? It was the Minister for International Trade. Then the Government has the gall, the colossal nerve, when we are asking very legitimate questions about what is going to happen if we go ahead with free trade negotiations without protecting Canadians and asking who will be hurt, to answer with scare tactics and give us a smear campaign that we are speaking only for labour. Nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister for International Trade and the Secretary of State for External Affairs know that this is a fact. They know that more and more people and more and more groups are expressing opposition or asking some very important questions which need to be answered.
We are for enhanced trade. That is why we support it and have always supported the Auto Pact. If we are going to look at each sector of our economy to try to work arrangements with the USA, or Japan, the EEC or anybody else that will bring advantages to us and them, we are all for it. What we are opposed to is this blind rush to do things without looking at the real situation.
The Government knows because the departmental officials in External Affairs have done their job. They have given reports to the Government, about which the Government does not talk, which the Government would prefer to hide, which tell in detail the things the Americans do to protect their people, their jobs and their industries. It is this whole "buy American" policy. Why doesn't the Minister for Internationa! Trade and that great negotiator, Mr. Simon Reisman, come clean with Canadians? Why don't they tell Canadians: "Look, we are going to try to negotiate better trading arrangements with the U.S., but you have to know not only that there are 600 Bills before Congress calling for more protection, but the U.S. has since 1933 had policies to protect the United States market for Americans"? Even if we get a free trade agreement, Mr. Speaker, the ability of American states to hinder trade not only between Canada and the USA but between American states to protect their markets will still be there.
Adjournment Debate
If we are going to have a serious, honest discussion on free trade, let the Government be honest. Let the Government tell Canadians what is involved. Let the Government tell Canadians about the benefits they will get but also about the harm that will be done to individuals and to many groups unless the Government of Canada is vigilant, tough and negotiates as an equal, not as a supplicant to the Americans. We cannot be telling the Americans that we will do anything as long as they give us a few bones to chew on.

subtopic: HOUSING-FUNDING OF PROGRAMS. (B) EXTENSION OF 1985 PROGRAMS-INTERIM FUNDING
HOUSING-FUNDING OF PROGRAMS. (B) EXTENSION OF 1985 PROGRAMS-INTERIM FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in December, 1985, the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight), who is responsible for CMHC, announced in the House of Commons a new housing program. A National Direction for Housing Solutions outlined five major program areas, but provided no details. It is now May 13 and not one of these programs is in place. Not one bit of federal money has gone toward the building of one housing unit so desperately needed in Canada.
On May 5 I asked the Minister in this House where the new housing programs are which he promised. Five months into 1986 he answered:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is apparent. Due to the change in delivery and cost sharing, effective in 1986, operating agreements with the provincial housing corporations have to be negotiated.
With all due respect, that answer is not apparent. What kind of Minister plans a year's housing programs which, almost half way through the year, are not in place because he still has to get agreement on the very housing programs that he wants to use?
On May 5 I also asked in this House whether, acting on precedent, the Minister could have either extended 1985 programs or provided interim funding for projects which are ready to go. When it became apparent that these agreements were not going to be negotiated until early in 1986, why the Minister did not bring forward a contingency plan for this year's housing. Why did he not extend the Section 56.1 program or the RRAP program until the negotiations were finalized?

May 13, 1986
Adjournment Debate
The consequences of this delay are almost criminal. In Toronto, city delivery agents have been anxiously awaiting the announcements and the budgets for the RRAP programs since December. On the homeowner and disabled program, they were told funding would come through early in April. It did not. There are real emergencies which are not being dealt with. In Toronto the municipal delivery agents, such as the Nonprofit Housing Corporation, are on the verge of sending applicants to apply under the provincial renovations programs in Ontario, which are not nearly as good as the federal program for homeowners, because they have no idea when the federal RRAP budget is coming through. Month after month it was promised that the money is coming, the application forms are coming, and the criteria are coming, but only rumours come.
An example of the tragic consequences of the delay is a disabled man in Toronto who has requested RRAP assistance in order to get his motorized wheelchair out of his home. Recently he has had to go to the hospital three days a week and, because he has not had the RRAP assistance to make his home accessible, he must pay out of his meagre pension to take a taxi each time.
The consequences do not stop there. The entire building season in northern Manitoba may well have been lost because building materials would have had to be transported in on the winter roads. They will now have to wait until next year. Those co-ops and non-profit groups which may be so lucky as to one day get start-up funds will, in all likelihood, be building next fall and winter and paying premium rates for heated concrete and any number of expensive alterations to building procedures to cope with the cold weather. The money spent on this will obviously be taken out of the other aspects of the design which might have added to the comfort and quality of the housing. It may even reduce the number of units built. This money is to pay for the Minister's delay.
I suggest that the Minister has been almost criminally negligent. Homeless people died in Toronto. An evicted tenant committed suicide in Vancouver. The answer to the pleas for someone to pay attention to the needs of Canadians desperate for housing was met time and time again in the House of Commons with the answer that the negotiations were ongoing with the provinces and a bigger and better housing program for needy Canadians was at hand, if they live that long.
I also suggest that the Minister and CMHC officials continue to mislead Members of Parliament and the public about these programs, however unintentionally. Last week my office received a notice from the Minister announcing that he had authorized the release of the 1986 RRAP budget. That is false. As of today no delivery agents have been told this. Even in his announcement he states that "CMHC will be in touch with local municipalities and delivery agents shortly to inform them of their homeowner RRAP allocations". "Shortly" is not "now". That program has not started. He states further that "the rental RRAP and the RRAP for the disabled will be delivered once the appropriate regulatory changes are
obtained. I expect these will be finalized shortly". "Shortly", again, is not "now". Since this is the same thing as he has been saying since December, can we expect to wait for another five months?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-FUNDING OF PROGRAMS. (B) EXTENSION OF 1985 PROGRAMS-INTERIM FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister and his officials are now completing what has been a most extensive and productive consultation and negotiation process on new housing directions which will focus on assisting those Canadians most in need. This lengthy process has meant meetings with the provinces and many representatives of housing interest groups, non-profit associations, native organizations and the real estate and building industry. As well, over 300 written briefs have been reviewed.
Over the past few months, planning and negotiations with the provinces have resulted in the implementation of social housing programs that both maintain federal objectives and meet the identified needs of the various provinces and territories. Most important, the provincial cost-sharing arrangements, along with targeting to households in core need, will more than double the number of housing units produced this year for those who must pay more than 30 per cent of their income for suitable, adequate accommodation.
At times, the negotiations have been complex, but the Minister is pleased to advise that eight global agreements have already been signed outlining the partnership arrangements between the federal and provincial Governments. In addition, detailed operating agreements have been signed with two of the provinces, and the final agreements should all be completed in the next few weeks. The Minister has authorized the release of the budgets of the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program for home owners and native people on-reserve to repair their houses. The remaining RRAP budgets will be allocated very shortly. The Minister would like this House to know as well that the Co-operative Housing Program is well under way. Sponsoring groups are submitting projects, and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials are in the process of selecting those that will proceed in 1986. Proposal development funding has been made available to groups to assist them.
All in all, implementation of the programs is progressing well and we expect to complete all the arrangements within the next few weeks.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-PRIVATE ENTERPRISE DOOR-TO-DOOR DELIVERY
CANADA POST CORPORATION-PRIVATE ENTERPRISE DOOR-TO-DOOR DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to pursue a question I put to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister responsible for Canada Post (Mr. Domm) on February 25 concerning the delivery of mail. I asked whether or not Canada Post would be encouraged to contract out more of its services in order to reduce the Corporation's costs and increase its efficiency. I also pointed
May 13, 1986

out that many Canadians who do not receive door-to-door delivery are hiring enterprising young people to pick up their mail from community boxes and deliver it to their homes on a daily basis.
Just last weekend I noticed an article in the Ottawa Citizen which profiled a local entrepreneur who has begun this kind of service for a monthly fee of less than $12. I believe this is an excellent initiative, and I certainly hope Canada Post officials will encourage more enthusiastic business people to undertake the same service in other communities. Had the Speaker afforded me the opportunity on February 25 to put a supplementary question, it would have concerned whether the extra amount paid by Canadians to obtain adequate door-to-door mail delivery service could be tax deductible. I look forward to speaking about that at another time.
Canadians are well aware of the serious problems facing Canada Post. Despite a five-year deficit reduction program which was to have eliminated Government subsidies by this year, Canada Post continues to mount severe losses. In 1985 this loss amounted to well over $300 million. Projections indicate that further deficits will continue. The Marchment report highlighted a number of other problems such as service, delivery, labour relations, financing and management.
In the recent federal Budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated that the Government is determined to come to grips with the financial and operating problems of Canada Post. The Government has also indicated that the corporation will be required to develop a new operating plan to improve productivity in order to reduce its operating deficit to zero by the end of fiscal year 1987-88.
I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary if that plan is now in place and if it includes greater contracting out of services. In addition, I trust that entrepreneurs will be allowed and encouraged to provide delivery service door-to-door from community boxes. I understand that this kind of service may involve a violation of the "exclusive right" privilege Canada Post enjoys to collect and deliver mail. If so, I would suggest that it is time to redefine that "exclusive right" privilege in order to increase the competition of mail delivery.
If this country is to enjoy effective and efficient mail delivery, we must meet the challenge of improving Canada Post. It is time to take immediate action to reduce costs by
Adjournment Debate
contracting out services and introducing greater private sector opportunities in mail delivery.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-PRIVATE ENTERPRISE DOOR-TO-DOOR DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post has the mandate to provide Canadians with convenient and efficient service at a reasonable cost. Over the last three years, the corporation has extended door-to-door mail delivery to over 340,000 addresses in Canada.
Last June, the corporation announced plans to upgrade delivery service to more than 200,000 additional addresses during the current fiscal year by readjusting letter carrier routes or by providing mail delivery through group mailboxes or community mailboxes.
These initiatives clearly demonstrate the corporation's concern in providing convenient service to all its customers and achieving financial self-sufficiency as requested by its shareholder, the Government of Canada.
These alternate means of mail delivery-group mailboxes and community mailboxes-are not exclusive to Canada. While these alternate modes of delivery offer convenience to customers and contribute substantially to reduce the deficit of Canada Post, it is understandable that some private citizens might want to contract the delivery of their mail from the postal station or group mailbox directly to their home.
Although Canada Post does not support such a service, principally on the grounds of security of the mail, it cannot refuse to hand over the mail to a third party when authorization that can be verified has been given by the customer.
It should, however, be clear that these particular arrangements are made solely between these individual contractors and their clients, and that Canada Post is not part of the contract. The corporation's responsibility for ensuring the security of the mail extends only to the point of delivery, should it be a local postal station, a lock box, a group mailbox or a community mailbox.
